extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and patent litigants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating sufficiency of patent specifications, admissible evidence (including expert testimony), the division of functions between court and jury, and principles for construing the scope of claims (novelty, utility, prior use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification addressed to persons skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is to be presumed addressed to competent practical workmen of ordinary skill in the art or science under which the patented invention falls; sufficiency must be referred to their ability to understand and apply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific witnesses may be examined on clearness and fulness, but the specification cannot be supplemented by a scientific person's fresh invention and correction. When the specification benefits a particular trade, evidence is limited to the ordinary knowledge and skill common to that trade. Example: where an invention requires engineering judgment (e.g., determining an angle for paddle-wheels), the specification may be presumed addressed to engineers capable of applying those principles and must furnish rules by which they can ascertain the parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must not require more than ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: When framing his specification the patentee must not call upon the persons to whom it is addressed to exercise more than the actual existing knowledge common to their trade or profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He may exhaust the trade's knowledge, but if following the directions would require the exercise of ingenuity or invention beyond ordinary competent skill (i.e., solving a new problem), the specification is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement = identity of the defendant's thing with the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: On infringement the point to determine is whether the thing made or used by the defendant is, in the sense of the patent law, identical with the patentee's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the same sort of inquiry as novelty — whether the alleged infringing thing is the same as or different from the patented thing — and is a mixed question of law and fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts may give two kinds of evidence: (1) point out and explain actual resemblances or differences (matters of fact observed by the senses), and (2) state opinions whether those differences or resemblances are material (opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The boundary between fact and opinion is often shadowy; courts must admit proper factual and opinion evidence without allowing the witness to decide the issue. Experts should not usurp the court's legal function of determining whether differences amount to a fresh invention. Their opinions are 'entitled to great respect' but the jury (or court) must decide the ultimate question under judicial instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court must instruct on legal standards (identity, fresh invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether two things are identical in the sense of patent law is a mixed question of law and fact; after differences or resemblances are ascertained, the court must instruct the jury what constitutes, in point of law, a difference or identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty of giving this instruction should not be surrendered by the court. Scientific witnesses can opine on importance of differences, but whether a change 'amounts, in point of law, to a change of the principle of the machine' is for the court to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior invention/use must be positive and procedurally noticed
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence for the defendant on novelty consists of positive proof that the thing patented existed before; if credible, it outweighs negative evidence offered by plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant who relies on prior invention, knowledge, or use must give notice of the names and residences of persons he intends to prove had prior knowledge or use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of witnesses with an interest or prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who have used the patented machine are not thereby rendered incompetent as witnesses on account of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a patentee in another patent who sold rights may be competent; an assignee or licensee may be competent (though interest affects weight). Evidence that prior users paid the plaintiff for licenses should not be absolutely rejected but may be given little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is principally a question of fact for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of novelty embraces whether the patentee was the inventor and whether the thing patented is substantially different from anything before known; these are questions of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is for the court, however, to instruct the jury what constitutes novelty in law and what sufficiency of invention is required to support a patent. Prior public use is likewise a question of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a renewed patent is for the same invention and abandonment are facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a renewed patent covers the same invention as the original, and whether the invention was abandoned to the public, are questions of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These issues should be decided on the evidence presented at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility: legal vs factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility can be impeached in two modes: (1) if the patent on its face shows the invention is injurious to morals/health (not a patentable subject) — a question of law; (2) if evidence shows the thing, although innocuous, is not capable of accomplishing its professed object — a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'useful invention' means not injurious/mischievous and not frivolous or insignificant but capable of some practical use. Degree of usefulness is unimportant; but if any essential thing claimed is wholly useless the patent is invalid for total failure of usefulness. Determinations of capability in practice depend on evidence and are for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frivolous or insignificant inventions are questions of law
rubrics_metrics.description: If the object proposed is frivolous or insignificant, from which no advantage can be derived to the public, the patent is void as not being for a patentable subject — a question of law for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the object is not clearly frivolous but the means fail in practice, the inquiry reverts to usefulness (a factual question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the specification/extent of the claim is for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of the specification as to the extent of the claim belongs to the province of the court; the court must determine what the claim actually covers and whether the patent is valid in point of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury take the court's construction and determine whether anything included in the claim is not new. If terms of art require explanation by evidence, the jury may find their meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for claim construction: descriptive parts and the patentee's actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may resort to the descriptive parts of the specification to inquire what the patentee has said he had invented; if that description is clear, the claim language should be construed to include the actual invention set forth, if consistent with principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general maxim is ut res magis valeat quam pereat — give the patent a construction that upholds it if practicable without violating sound principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: When description is uncertain, consider evidence (state of the art and actual invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the descriptive parts are uncertain without evidence, the court should attend to what evidence shows is new or old, the state of the art, and whether the patentee discovered a general principle or only a form of applying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inquiry determines whether the patentee can claim the application of a principle broadly under other forms or is confined to specific forms and methods he described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court entitled to receive evidence of the actual invention and to inform itself
rubrics_metrics.description: In a trial the state of the art and facts about the inventor's surroundings will be developed; in determining the claim's meaning the judge must 'gather as he goes along,' informing himself on the evidence and observing controverted facts bearing upon claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If facts material to construction are not in doubt, the court gives construction absolutely; if evidence requires factual findings, the construction is given conditionally for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee presumed not to intend to claim things known in use
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is manifest from the terms that the patentee has included something of which he was not the inventor, his patent cannot cover it; the patentee is presumed not to intend to claim things he must know to be in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The degree to which a prior-known thing was familiar and in constant use is important in deciding whether the patentee intended to claim it; read the specification to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery consistent with fair import of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art limits broad/general terms in specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: General terms in a specification will be interpreted to include only substances ejusdem generis with particular substances mentioned that may reasonably be supposed, on the state of the art, to have been contemplated at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a gas apparatus described to extract gas 'from pit coal, or tar, or any other substance' was interpreted to mean those substances in actual or reasonable use for the purpose at the patent date (oil being known to yield gas but not then expected to be used for illumination because too expensive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction may rest on facts incorporated into the description; court takes notice if proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification refers to facts as part of the description which govern construction, if those facts are proved or admitted the court will take notice of them in giving a legal construction; if controverted they go to the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a case about 'bow-flyers' the court took notice of admitted facts showing the bow-flyer alone was intended because the description and gearing corresponded only to that form. When such facts are without dispute the court must give legal construction accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and certainty of description: liberal construction but public notice required
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification should describe the invention with reasonable certainty so others can know whether they violate the patent and, after expiry, can make machines correctly; but courts give a liberal construction to sustain inventors if practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: Act of Congress requires particular specification and pointing of the part claimed; public must be able to know the scope. Courts should encourage ingenuity by protecting legitimate inventions, yet not allow monopolies of what belonged to others or the public.
